2026-10-28DecisionAnalysis available

FOMC statement · October rate decision

Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

Read analysis

The FOMC held the federal funds target at 3.75–4.00% by a 10–2 vote. Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack preferred a quarter-point increase. The statement characterised activity as strong, spending as resilient, investment as robust, and unemployment as little changed. It flagged elevated inflation and framed further information as useful to assessing the stance needed to return to 2%. The dissents establish a debate over whether to tighten immediately. The release gives 2 p.m. EDT as the event timestamp.

Questions for further research

  1. Did the hold and dissents shift the next meeting’s pricing? Measure changes in meeting-dated futures or OIS around 2 p.m. EDT and distinguish the statement window from the press conference.
  2. Which incoming information could move the majority toward a hike? Compare the next inflation and employment prints with the statement's description.
  3. Was yield-curve movement driven by the policy path or duration pricing? Compare 2Y Treasuries, near-term OIS and longer yields inside the same release window.

Source sections: Release time, policy decision, activity and inflation paragraphs, voting record

Official source ↗

2026-10-28StatementAnalysis available

FOMC press conference · October meeting

Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

Read analysis

Warsh described real activity as improving while inflation remained too high, with a risk that sector-specific price changes could spread. In response to questions about the hold, he framed policy around the broader strategy and incoming information. He defended the 2% target and discussed anchoring expectations, while his responses left the timing of the next decision contingent. The Q&A contains the reporters’ descriptions of market and household expectations, which should be read as questions unless separately supported.

He also announced a planned format change in 2027, with one of eight meetings devoted to strategy and no rate vote or statement anticipated for that meeting. That institutional change is distinct from the October decision. The value of the press conference for event analysis is the clarification delivered after the statement at a separate time.

Questions for further research

  1. Did discussion of the hold add information beyond the written statement? Compare the press-conference window and the 2 p.m. statement window in meeting-dated futures.
  2. How anchored were longer-run expectations at the time? Compare contemporaneous household surveys, inflation compensation and the cited policy discussion.
  3. How might the revised meeting schedule show up in pricing? Compare contracts spanning the strategy meeting and neighbouring rate-setting meetings.

Source sections: Transcript opening remarks and Q&A on the hold, expectations, strategy and the 2027 schedule

2026-10-28StatementAnalysis available

FOMC implementation note

Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

Read analysis

The Fed set out how the Desk would maintain the 3.75–4.00% target range. The note describes overnight repo and reverse repo terms, rolling Treasury principal, reinvesting agency principal into Treasury bills, and conditional purchases aimed at keeping reserves ample. The primary credit rate remained 4.0%. The operating instructions provide a basis for tracking implementation and money-market conditions separately from the FOMC’s inflation and growth assessment.

Questions for further research

  1. Are overnight rates staying within the desired range? Compare EFFR, repurchase rates and facility use around reporting and settlement dates.
  2. What volumes of short-dated purchases are actually conducted? Check the Desk’s public schedules and operations against balance-sheet data.
  3. Does reserve distribution explain funding pressure? Compare dispersion in funding rates and facility take-up with aggregate reserve balances.

Source sections: Interest on reserve balances, Desk directive and primary credit rate

2026-10-14SpeechAnalysis available

Michelle Bowman · Supervisory Modernization After Silicon Valley Bank

Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

Read analysis

Bowman used the 2023 banking stress review to make a case for clearer escalation and a focus on risks capable of causing material harm. The revised operating principles emphasise supervisory judgement, early identification and timely intervention. She tied those lessons to the FSB’s work on aligning supervisory intensity with size, complexity and interconnectedness. Her policy proposal concerns supervision. The implications for funding resilience depend on how quickly examiners identify exposures and how institutions respond.

Questions for further research

  1. Would earlier escalation have revealed concentrated funding risk? Trace independent-review findings against stress signals and contemporaneous supervisor actions.
  2. How will examiners distinguish material interest-rate and liquidity risk? Compare revised supervisory guidance against the balance-sheet exposures it targets.
  3. Could banks respond by changing funding or duration? Track deposit concentration, hedges and liquidity buffers after implementation.

Source sections: Independent review findings, revised operating principles and Financial Stability Board discussion

2026-10-14ResearchAnalysis available

Beige Book · national summary

Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

Read analysis

Two of twelve districts reported moderate growth, three modest growth, four slight growth and three little change. The report describes stronger manufacturing in Dallas and growth in factories across several other districts, paired with a more restrained outlook. Some employers reported slower workforce expansion as AI improved productivity. Contacts described diesel and other input costs flowing through supply chains while consumers resisted retail price increases. Firms reported selective pass-through, promotions and cost adjustments, so the price evidence points to pressure on margins as well as selling prices. This is qualitative evidence from district contacts.

Questions for further research

  1. How broad is the factory upturn? Cross-check district reports with industrial production and new orders by industry.
  2. Does diesel pass-through spread to consumer categories? Compare freight surcharges, producer prices and subsequent retail prices by goods category.
  3. How much employment restraint reflects AI adoption? Compare firm responses on staffing, vacancies and output with payroll and hiring series.

Source sections: Overall Economic Activity, Labor Markets, Prices and district highlights

2026-10-08SpeechAnalysis available

Christopher Waller · The Signaling Value of the Summary of Economic Projections

Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

Read analysis

Waller attributed his support for September’s quarter-point increase to a shift in risks over several months. Labour conditions had stabilised and inflation remained above target. He cited August core PCE inflation of 3% year over year and judged that returning inflation to target required further hikes if incoming data followed his baseline.

He argued that the Fed can signal the likely extent of tightening and leave its timing contingent on the data. His three-hike example illustrates the communication mechanism. September’s projections put at least one more 2026 hike in 16 of 18 participants’ submissions, while his account of the previous day’s fed funds futures shows the market attaching a range of probabilities to the timing and number of moves. The market pricing he cites was available before the speech.

Questions for further research

  1. What did the speech add to the path already priced? Check meeting-dated futures around the verified first public release and compare with the prior day's curve.
  2. Which inflation data would change the pace of tightening? Compare incoming core PCE components and employment data with Waller’s stated baseline.
  3. What does dispersion among the dots hide? Compare the September SEP’s end-year points with futures pricing at individual meetings.

Source sections: Economic update, communication examples, September SEP and market-pricing discussion, footnote 1

Official source ↗

2026-10-07MinutesAnalysis available

FOMC minutes · September 15–16 meeting

Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

Read analysis

The minutes document September’s unanimous quarter-point increase to 3.75–4.00%, released to the public on October 7. The statement recorded resilient spending, strong capital investment and limited change in unemployment alongside above-target inflation. The domestic directive maintained the ample-reserves framework, allowing purchases of Treasury bills and, as needed, short-dated Treasuries. For market work, the time of the September rate announcement and the October minutes release are distinct events.

Questions for further research

  1. How much of the rationale was already public? Compare the September statement, press conference and projections with the detail first published in the minutes.
  2. Did the minutes affect the expected pace of tightening? Use meeting-dated futures around 2 p.m. ET on October 7 and check other scheduled releases.
  3. How do reserves purchases differ from shifts in policy stance? Check Desk purchase schedules and reserve measures alongside the directive and policy-rate expectations.

Source sections: Participants’ views, committee policy actions, domestic policy directive

2026-10-06SpeechAnalysis available

Michelle Bowman · Modernizing the Regulatory and Supervisory Landscape

Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

Read analysis

Bowman proposed using risk and complexity, alongside asset size, to determine supervisory intensity. The speech describes how fixed thresholds can move a conventional lender into standards intended for more complex firms. She linked threshold modernisation, proportionality and faster identification of material risks. The speech discusses changes already made to supervisory principles alongside future reforms under consideration. The latter should be tracked through rulemaking before assessing their effect on credit availability or bank capital.

Questions for further research

  1. Which firms face the largest threshold effects? Map public bank sizes and activities to the proposed categories as proposals become available.
  2. Would lighter reporting increase lending capacity? Compare costs and lending decisions around relevant thresholds and implementation dates.
  3. Can earlier supervisory action preserve resilience? Assess escalation timing and material findings across comparable supervisory cases.

Source sections: Regulatory thresholds and Refocusing Supervision on the Risk of Material Financial Harm

2026-10-01SpeechAnalysis available

Philip Jefferson · The U.S. Economy and Monetary Policy

Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

Read analysis

Jefferson saw continued resilience in activity and employment but judged the inflation risk to be skewed upward. Figure 1 puts first-half GDP growth at a 2.4% annual pace. He noted robust AI investment and resilient spending, with price sensitivity among consumers and uncertainty from energy, tariffs and the scope of the AI buildout. Figure 3 shows unemployment had moved roughly sideways in 2026 and fell to 4.1% in August, a level he regarded as close to maximum employment.

The PCE charts distinguish total inflation from core inflation and split core goods from services. Jefferson considered several shocks jointly and thought it premature to specify the policy path after September’s increase. He noted yields had risen since the meeting, but the speech does not measure a move attributable to the remarks. The views are his own.

Questions for further research

  1. Which components explain the acceleration in core prices? Check the next PCE release against figures 6 and 7 and separate goods and service contributions.
  2. How concentrated is growth in AI capital expenditure? Use GDP expenditure details and capital-spending disclosures to test the resilience of demand.
  3. How much tightening did markets already expect? Compare the pre-speech fed funds futures curve with the September policy path and verified event-time changes.

Source sections: Economic Activity and the Labor Market, Inflation, Monetary Policy, figures 1–8 and accessible chart tables

Official source ↗ · Accessible chart tables ↗

2026-10-01SpeechAnalysis available

Michelle Bowman · Modernizing Financial Regulation: Initial Observations from eSLR

Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

Read analysis

Bowman argued that the supplementary leverage requirement had become a binding constraint for some large bank dealers and that recalibration could support balance-sheet-intensive Treasury intermediation. She cited supervisory data showing dealer Treasury holdings rose from about $600 billion to over $700 billion by the end of April, with more growth among banks that had smaller buffers under the prior rule.

She also cited market outreach and indicators such as narrower spreads and lower volatility around auctions. These are preliminary observations, and the reported change in holdings has a different evidentiary status from statements by individual market contacts. The suggested mechanism is more capacity for dealers to absorb Treasury supply, with implications for liquidity and cash–futures positioning.

Questions for further research

  1. Can holdings growth be attributed to the calibration? Compare affected and less constrained dealers, conditioning on issuance and market volatility.
  2. Does capacity remain available in stress? Compare quote depth, repo terms and dealer holdings on the busiest auction or volatility days.
  3. How has exposure moved between dealers and leveraged funds? Cross-check Treasury positions, repo funding and futures exposures over the same period.

Source sections: Binding leverage requirements, supervisory data, market outreach and footnotes

Official source ↗

Canada

2026-10-28ForecastAnalysis available

Monetary Policy Report—October 2026

Bank of Canada

Read analysis

The October outlook projects inflation above 3% through much of 2027 and near 2% by mid-2028. The Bank judged that sustained oil and refinery pressures were affecting Canadian firms’ costs, with broader consumer-price effects expected as those costs passed through. The same energy shock supports investment and exports through Canada’s commodity sector while reducing purchasing power for households and raising costs for energy users.

The Bank forecasts 1% annual growth in 2026 and 2% in both 2027 and 2028. Stronger midyear activity improved the growth outlook versus July. Tariffs and uncertainty still constrain exports and investment in affected sectors, while housing remains weak. The report’s outlook is conditional on its trade, energy and pass-through assumptions.

Questions for further research

  1. What would bring CPI back to target faster? Re-run the report’s assumption with a faster fall in oil and refinery margins, then check whether pricing behaviour changes.
  2. How exposed is the growth upgrade to tariffs? Track trade by industry, capital spending plans and US demand in the sectors identified by the report.
  3. Is housing the main source of downside growth risk? Compare mortgage renewals, resale activity and residential investment with the report’s projected path.

Source sections: Overview and report chapters on outlook and risks

Coverage: Executive overview and forecast narrative. Underlying chart data and linked technical material have not been fully reviewed.

Official source ↗

2026-10-28DecisionAnalysis available

Bank of Canada raises the policy rate by 25 basis points to 2½%

Bank of Canada

Read analysis

The Bank raised the overnight-rate target to 2.50%, with the Bank Rate at 2.75% and the deposit rate at 2.45%. Persistently high energy prices and refinery margins had kept headline inflation near 3% since April. The Bank saw signs of broader cost pressures, including transport and imported industrial and electronics inputs. Core measures remained near 2%, but its surveys indicated more firms expected to pass through higher input costs.

The Canadian economy also entered the second half of 2026 stronger than the Bank had forecast in July. The Bank nevertheless projected a tariff-related slowdown in the fourth quarter and described some excess supply. The decision addresses the risk of persistent inflation as activity recovers, with the next steps contingent on incoming data. The release describes recent rates and currency conditions without providing an event-window market response.

Questions for further research

  1. How fast are input costs reaching consumer prices? Use the Bank’s business surveys and CPI component contributions to distinguish direct gasoline effects from broader pass-through.
  2. How much has domestic slack narrowed? Compare job vacancies, hours worked and output-gap estimates with the October forecast.
  3. How much tightening was priced before the release? Match the original release time to CORRA pricing and CAD observations around the announcement.

Source sections: Rate decision, Canadian outlook and inflation paragraphs

2026-10-23SpeechAnalysis available

Jonathan Heath · Mexico’s Inflation and Monetary Policy Outlook

Banco de México

Read analysis

Heath’s deck compared headline and core inflation with the 3% target. The annual headline chart shows an increase from the mid-2026 low to 3.45% in September. The core exhibits provide a separate view of underlying prices, with different movements visible from the headline line. Reading the latest headline point alone would miss the composition of the remaining inflation gap.

The real rate figure subtracts survey expectations over the coming 12 months from the overnight policy target. Its shaded band is Banxico’s estimated long-run neutral range, not a directly observed market value. For a policy-path assessment, the exhibit frames how a change in either expected inflation or the policy target can change the real stance.

Questions for further research

  1. Which components account for the latest change in annual inflation? Compare component contributions, seasonally adjusted monthly rates and base effects.
  2. How sensitive is the stance to the expectation measure? Recalculate using the survey distribution, alternative horizons and the neutral range shown.
  3. Did investors reprice the timing of a policy change? Check Mexican front-end swaps with verified release timing and earlier communications.

Source sections: Headline and Core annual inflation charts, neutral and ex ante real short-term rate chart

Coverage: Analysis covers the named slides in the official deck. The archive date is the date Banxico lists for the presentation.

2026-10-08MinutesAnalysis available

Minutes of the policy decision announced on 24 September 2026

Banco de México

Read analysis

The board unanimously left its overnight interbank target at 6.50% in September. The published minutes present the September hold as a decision to evaluate how ongoing disinflation, spare capacity and the existing degree of monetary restraint interact. Currency pass-through and inflation expectations were central to the next decision. The board stressed that Mexican conditions could justify a different response from the Federal Reserve.

The relevant distinction for a rates event study is between the September decision and information about the reaction function disclosed when the minutes came out in October. Rate or FX moves around those releases would answer different questions.

Questions for further research

  1. What would make an easing decision compatible with still-elevated inflation expectations? Compare core price composition and survey expectations with the board’s disinflation criteria.
  2. How strong is MXN pass-through under spare capacity? Test regional import-price and CPI categories against MXN changes and measures of domestic slack.
  3. What fresh information did investors get in October? Compare the September statement to the minutes and check short-dated swaps around the minutes release.

Source sections: Sections 3–4, policy decision and vote

Colombia

2 sources · 2 notes
2026-10-30DecisionAnalysis available

Board holds the policy rate at 12.25% by majority vote

Banco de la República

Read analysis

Four directors voted to retain the 12.25% policy rate and three preferred a 25 basis point increase. Annual September headline inflation edged up to 6.3%, while core inflation excluding food and regulated prices fell to 6.0% from 6.1%. Analyst expectations for the end of 2026 edged higher to 6.9%, and two-year expectations remained near 4.0%. Measures inferred from government debt remained away from the 3% target.

The release describes the rate as restrictive and consistent with declining inflation in 2027. Recent activity data pointed to weaker growth, partly related to lower consumption growth and the earthquake. El Niño and the fiscal outlook remained material risks. The vote leaves a live policy split over whether the current level suffices and does not establish the market surprise.

Questions for further research

  1. Which incoming inflation measures would tip the balance toward another hike? Check whether lower core inflation persists alongside the food and regulated components highlighted in the statement.
  2. Is weaker activity broad or driven by temporary events? Compare national activity data with geography and sector exposure to the earthquake.
  3. Could fiscal changes affect the yield curve independently of policy expectations? Compare fiscal announcements, local swap pricing and TES term structure.

Source sections: Decision, voting split and inflation and activity bullets

Official source ↗

2026-10-05MinutesAnalysis available

September policy meeting minutes: increase of 25 basis points to 12.25%

Banco de la República

Read analysis

The October release records a divided September rate increase. Four directors chose a 25 basis point increase to 12.25%, two preferred a hold and one wanted a 50 basis point increase. The majority cited broad price pressure, with annual headline inflation at 6.2% in August and inflation excluding food and regulated prices at 6.1%. It worried that El Niño and international energy or input costs could prolong inflation and affect expectations.

The hold voters argued that policy was already markedly restrictive and that past increases were still feeding through. They also noted that another hike would have a limited short-run effect on administered, food and indexed prices while increasing costs to credit, activity and post-earthquake reconstruction. July activity indicators already pointed to a slowdown, yet retail sales were still growing in annual terms.

Questions for further research

  1. Is disinflation held back by indexation or excess demand? Compare rents and regulated-price adjustments with cyclical and non-cyclical services prices.
  2. How fast is cumulative tightening reaching households and firms? Track the evolution of new loan rates and issuance by type alongside the rate path and reconstruction activity.
  3. Can survey and market measures corroborate de-anchoring? Compare survey forecasts with nominal and inflation-linked TES pricing after adjusting for liquidity.

Source sections: Vote counts, policy arguments and updated activity indicators

Coverage: Main minutes text reviewed. Statistical appendix and separate capital-markets attachment are outside this card.

2026-10-09SpeechAnalysis available

When the policy mix meets supply shocks — Agnès Bénassy-Quéré

Banque de France

Read analysis

Bénassy-Quéré argued that supply shocks complicate coordination because inflation rises as output weakens. Temporary energy support can cushion incomes and reduce the measured CPI peak, while broad fiscal support can sustain demand and increase financing pressure. Higher nominal growth does not guarantee improved fiscal space when spending is indexed and debt service rises. Support that eases a bottleneck can affect inflation differently from general demand support.

France’s energy shield is the main case study. The Banque de France research cited in the speech estimates that the shield reduced inflation by around 2.6 percentage points in 2022. Part of that effect reversed in subsequent years. The evidence leaves open whether a lower peak also moderated wage and expectation persistence. Comparisons between French and aggregate euro area prices are descriptive and cannot identify the shield’s full long-run impact on their own.

Questions for further research

  1. How much of the lower measured inflation reflected postponed price increases? Review the shield study’s counterfactual, regulated tariff schedules and pass-through after support was wound back.
  2. Did a lower inflation peak change bargained wages and expectations? Compare sector wage deals, household expectations and cross-country evidence controlling for other shocks.
  3. What is the cost of financing renewed support? Assess the programme’s primary balance effect, debt maturity and sensitivity to long yields.

Source sections: Slides 5–8 and the France case study.

Read analysis

Greene’s concern was that UK labour market slack would provide less protection against persistent energy shock effects than the headline indicators suggested. Private sector regular average weekly earnings and tax payroll measures pointed to stalled wage disinflation. Her reading of the Decision Maker Panel, reported settlements and posted wages was that wage growth could settle nearer 3.5% than 3% over the coming year. She favoured leaning proactively against the risk. The staff scenarios she cited suggest that tightening against stronger second-round effects, then adjusting if they fail to materialise, can be less costly than discovering persistence after a weaker response. Bailey argued that the resilience of banks, borrowers and core markets gives policymakers room to respond to repeated supply shocks. The Governor’s autumn lecture: Why is the last mile of disinflation taking so long? — Ida Wolden Bache

Norges Bank

Read analysis

Bache asked why Norwegian inflation was still above target after the initial rise had subsided. She considered different speeds of price adjustment, wage and price formation in an open economy, and inflation expectations. A sequence of higher import prices can feed through gradually. Higher export prices can also improve exporters’ capacity to pay, allowing wage deals in the traded sector to support cost increases elsewhere. Coordinated bargaining therefore has different effects depending on whether the original shock mainly raises costs or strengthens the income of firms setting the wage norm.

A stylised model illustrates how higher foreign real rates can weaken the exchange-rate channel and how domestic real appreciation can damp imported price pressure. The calibrations are illustrations, with no estimated historical contribution for the individual mechanisms. Bache also observed that the decline in expectations had stalled and discussed the difficulty of separating the causal influence of expectations from other simultaneous developments.

Martin described tiering of interest on SNB sight deposits as a way to sustain trading in secured money markets while aligning SARON with the policy rate. The PBOC presents the renminbi as a managed float, based on market supply and demand with reference to a currency basket. It argues that the exchange rate responds to growth, monetary policy, markets and shocks, and that a current-account surplus by itself cannot identify a misaligned exchange rate. Its account points to multiple episodes of appreciation and depreciation as evidence of growing two-way flexibility. The bank attributes export competitiveness to structural factors and rejects competitive devaluation as a policy objective.

The paper is the issuing central bank’s position in a debate about exchange rate valuation. Its critique of using a single estimated equilibrium level is relevant for scenario analysis, because model assumptions can change a misalignment estimate. The publication does not supply a numerical exchange rate target or an observed price reaction to the statement.

Questions for further research

Read analysis

The study groups credit records by household using address information. Its panel includes about 2.06 million households, allowing it to track other household members’ credit alongside that of a primary borrower. The authors argue that individual records alone can miss exposure across people who share financial decisions. Their stress exercise estimates a broadly steady delinquency rate among borrowing households overall after a rate shock but a larger response for a defined set of highly leveraged homebuyers. For that subgroup, a 1 percentage point rise in rates was estimated to increase delinquency probability by 0.81 percentage points. The group is identified by the increase in debt service relative to income at purchase.

These are conditional estimates from a staff study. An aggregate result can conceal distributional tail risk and contagion among household members. The source does not imply that policy is committed to reining in credit solely through the policy rate.

Read analysis

The staff note distinguishes the IMF’s observed current account from its model-based benchmark. Korea’s surplus increased from 5.3% to 6.6% of GDP and the IMF External Balance Assessment norm fell from 4.7% to 3.3%; both widened the measured gap. The note estimates that the revision to the model, especially demographics, lowered Korea’s norm by 1.10 percentage points in a held-constant comparison. Most of that change showed up as an unexplained residual in the model. The authors question whether the revised specification captures Korea’s demographic structure. Robinson contrasts the immediate demand effects of AI investment and higher asset values with possible future supply gains that have yet to be demonstrated at scale. He uses the example of AI diffusing into local services to show how productivity could spread beyond tradables, reduce costs and increase the ability of workers to perform technically demanding tasks. The policy questions hinge on observed diffusion and whether investment is translating into productive capacity.

He cites MAS’s calibrated April and July tightening in the context of stronger activity and a projected wider output gap. For the future, his prescriptions are state contingent: demand pressure may warrant restraint early in the investment boom, while stronger verified productive capacity can change the balance later. The direction of the neutral rate is uncertain because better expected investment returns and precautionary saving could work in opposite directions. He argues that macroprudential policy has a role in addressing leverage built around uncertain future revenues. This speech provides an analytical framework without a dated change in the exchange-rate band.

Questions for further research

  1. Which indicators distinguish an investment boom from durable supply gains? Compare hardware and construction expenditure with measured services productivity and business adoption.
  2. How big is the leverage channel if expected AI earnings disappoint? Track project financing, issuer debt maturities and valuation sensitivity to revised revenues.
  3. What evidence would alter the estimated neutral exchange-rate path? Test productivity diffusion and domestic saving scenarios against the MAS macroeconomic assessment.

Despite the unchanged policy rate during the period covered, lending rates on new rupee loans had risen while new term deposit rates had declined through August. 2026-10-30StatementAnalysis available

Economic and Monetary Conditions for September and Q3 2026

Bank of Thailand

Read analysis

The Bank of Thailand reports that activity improved in September and over the third quarter. Technology-related merchandise exports and the flow of equipment for data centres supported investment and manufacturing. Tourism arrivals fell, particularly on short routes, although longer stays supported foreign tourism receipts. Services consumption softened in September amid cost-of-living pressures.

The September and quarterly inflation pictures differ. In September, higher retail energy prices raised headline inflation while fresh food and core inflation were broadly stable from the previous month. Looking across Q3 as a whole, headline inflation fell relative to the prior quarter as energy prices declined, while prepared-food prices contributed to firmer core inflation. The current account was in deficit in September but in surplus over the quarter. The release flags rising unemployment-benefit claims for monitoring despite broadly stable labour conditions.

Questions for further research

  1. Will technology exports lead to a broader improvement in domestic demand? Compare import content, investment volumes and employment in the sectors benefiting from data-centre activity.
  2. Are recent price increases reversing or spreading? Check monthly CPI changes across energy, prepared food and other services, and use the same comparison periods.
  3. Can tourism receipts remain stable with fewer arrivals? Compare nights stayed, daily spending and the composition of long- and short-haul groups.

Source sections: September detail and “Quarterly Review of the Thai Economy”; covers the release text.

Monetary Policy Committee’s Decision 5/2026

Bank of Thailand

Read analysis

The participating MPC members unanimously held the policy rate at 1.00%; one member was absent. The committee said an accommodative setting and targeted financial measures supported an uneven recovery. It expected the technology and AI cycle to support exports and investment, with GDP growth of 2.4% in 2026 and 2.1% in 2027. It judged output growth still below potential and benefits concentrated in the sectors most exposed to the cycle.

The bank expected temporary supply-driven inflation from energy and El Niño. Its projections put headline inflation at 2.1% in 2026 and 1.3% in 2027, while core inflation was 1.2% and 1.3%. The committee noted a weaker baht and somewhat higher government yields, while private loan costs remained broadly steady. Larger borrowers drove the pickup in loans as SME credit continued to contract. The combination explains why broader credit measures could look firm while some borrowers still faced financing constraints.

Questions for further research

  1. Could energy pass-through spread into core inflation despite weak demand? Compare domestic energy subsidies, corporate pricing and core CPI breadth under alternative oil paths.
  2. How broad is the technology-led recovery? Compare export and investment gains with sectoral employment and SME credit volumes.
  3. What explains the baht’s movement around the decision? Align the policy release with THB trading and check concurrent dollar and oil moves.

Source sections: Decision, growth and inflation projections, financial conditions and final policy paragraph.

Bullock told the Senate that recently realised upside risks would probably push inflation above the RBA’s August base case even as aggregate growth slowed. 2026-10-22ResearchAnalysis available

Perceived Monetary Policy Rules: Evidence From Professional Forecasters in Australia

Reserve Bank of Australia

Read analysis

The authors estimate how professional forecasters believed the RBA would react to economic conditions between 2015 and 2025. They map survey expectations for macro variables into rate forecasts with rules whose parameters vary over time. Before the pandemic, forecasters perceived a relatively modest inflation response, in part because they doubted low inflation would induce easing when policymakers stressed employment and financial stability. After COVID, belief in a stronger inflation response rose once tightening began in 2022.

Differences in projected economic conditions usually explained more rate disagreement than differences in the perceived reaction function, although disagreement about the response to higher inflation mattered in the post-pandemic episode. For a speech-monitoring project, the implication is that textual signals should be evaluated against both new macro evidence and the policy actions that establish credibility. The estimates reflect survey-implied beliefs of the forecaster sample and the paper’s specifications. They do not identify the RBA’s true policy rule or translate directly to live market pricing.

Questions for further research

  1. Does the result persist beyond professional economists’ surveys? Estimate analogous perceived responses from meeting-dated market prices and alternative surveys, with changes in risk compensation considered.
  2. How sensitive are the results to rule specification? Compare estimates with alternative horizons and macro inputs, including financial conditions and policy lags.
  3. When does communication lead followed policy? Line up narrative changes, forecast revisions and realised decisions around distinct inflation and activity shocks.

Source sections: Abstract, non-technical summary, estimated rules and cash-rate disagreement section

2026-10-16ResearchAnalysis available

Anthony Brassil and Michele Bullock: Overview of the RBA Annual Conference on Monetary Policy Trade-offs

Reserve Bank of Australia

Read analysis

Brassil and Bullock argue that the policy cost of returning inflation to target depends on the shock, the economy and the credibility of policy. A persistent adverse supply shock pushes prices up while weakening output and real income. Tightening can limit persistence but adds to near-term demand weakness. A slower return can lessen the immediate employment effects while increasing the chance that higher inflation becomes embedded.

The overview cautions that inflation costs are widespread and partly difficult to observe, such as the time spent seeking lower prices or renegotiating wages. Unemployment costs are concentrated and more visible and can have long-lived effects on workers’ skills and matches. The paper summarises contributions on measuring these costs and how anchored expectations change the trade-off. The macro use is in assessing the reaction to a particular shock and the distribution of adjustment costs. It is a conference overview.

Questions for further research

  1. What distinguishes a supply shock from a broad excess-demand episode in real time? Compare the joint behaviour of prices, output and employment by sector and use the conference papers’ identification approaches.
  2. Which indicators measure costly loss of inflation anchoring early enough to matter? Compare expectation horizons, firm price plans and wage contracts after previous cost shocks.
  3. Who bears the labour-market adjustment? Use household and labour microdata to examine job loss, duration, wage scars and consumption rather than relying on aggregate employment alone.

Source sections: Overview pp. 1–3. Conference 8–9 October, overview released 16 October.

Financial Stability Review, October 2026: financial stability assessment

Reserve Bank of Australia

Read analysis

The RBA assesses Australian banks and most household and business borrowers as resilient despite weakening activity and housing prices. Prudent underwriting and strong bank capital provide scope to absorb losses. The consequences of higher rates still vary by borrower, and the assessment identifies possible blind spots as non-bank lending expands and international risks rise.

The assessment connects rising global sovereign yields to policy repricing and competition for debt financing, including AI-related corporate issuance. 2026-10-28DecisionAnalysis available

OCR held at 2.75%: October Monetary Policy Review

Reserve Bank of New Zealand

Read analysis

The MPC voted 4–3 to hold at 2.75%. September-quarter annual CPI eased to 3.7% from 4.1%, a slightly better outcome than expected, while core measures were near the top of the 1–3% target range and increases had broadened. The December-quarter forecast was 4.4%, largely on fuel futures at the time of the review. The export recovery contrasted with weak domestic demand. The lower trade-weighted currency could add to imported costs, while weak demand limited how easily firms could pass these through.

The majority put more weight on subdued wage growth, anchored medium-term expectations and allowing time for two previous increases to work. The minority preferred a 25 basis point increase to 3%, pointing to inflation persistence and sufficient overall resilience to act. All members judged tighter policy likely, conditional on the outlook. The record explicitly leaves room to hold if domestic pricing cools and to ease if a severe global downturn materially changes the outlook. The divergence was about timing and risk, alongside agreement on the central direction.

Questions for further research

  1. Does domestic pricing broaden after accounting for imported fuel? Compare core and non-tradables subindices with wage growth, margins and business pricing intentions.
  2. How much of the decision was in NZD rates before publication? Check dated OIS or bank-bill quotes around the confirmed 2 pm New Zealand release and verify other overlapping news.
  3. Is export strength reaching households? Track regional employment, consumption and confidence alongside trade and tourism receipts.

Source sections: Media release and summary record, especially the conditional outlook and vote

Setting the scenario: Monetary policy communications in uncertain times

Bank of Canada

Read analysis

Deputy Governor Toni Gravelle explains how scenario analysis can communicate the Bank’s reaction function beyond a single central forecast. Longer borrowing rates respond to expected future policy rates, so explaining how policy could react to different shocks can influence financing conditions. The weight a scenario receives depends on the nature of the uncertainty. In extreme cases scenarios can replace a central forecast, while in normal settings selected cases complement it.

Gravelle describes the prolonged oil shock as an example. By the October decision, observed oil and inflation outcomes had tracked the April higher-for-longer scenario more closely than the April baseline. That experience supports communicating the risks around a forecast and what the Bank would watch. The speech explains a policy framework and refers to the earlier decision without setting a new rate path.

Questions for further research

  1. How far did the April energy scenario anticipate October outcomes? Compare the chart’s oil and inflation paths with the incoming data and the baseline published at the same time.
  2. Does scenario language change the expected path or mainly the tails? Compare CORRA and rate-option pricing around scenario publications, controlling for simultaneous forecast revisions.
  3. How does pass-through change across shocks? Use survey evidence and price decomposition to distinguish energy effects from wage and demand dynamics.

Banco de México lowered its overnight interbank target by 25 basis points to 6.25%, effective on 6 November. Three board members supported the cut and two voted for a hold. The minutes show why four directors paused and three favoured another 25 basis point hike. The dissenters judged another hike necessary to regain credibility and contain second-round effects. The minutes explain the 3–4 November decision to keep the Selic target at 13.75%. Copom described a sharper slowdown in cyclical activity and early cooling in the labour market, alongside accelerating headline and underlying inflation above the tolerance range. The external backdrop, including higher energy costs and tighter policy in advanced economies, added to uncertainty.

In the reference scenario the committee projected IPCA inflation at 5.6% for 2026, 4.7% for 2027 and 3.5% at the policy-relevant horizon in the second quarter of 2028. Schnabel argued for preserving policy flexibility when shocks are large, overlapping and persistent. She pointed to a rise in medium- to longer-term household inflation expectations in the wake of the latest energy shock, while identifying other shocks to demand and capacity linked to AI investment and fiscal spending.

These observations identify vulnerabilities and policy trade-offs rather than a meeting-specific rate recommendation.

The low-gear labour market — Clare Lombardelli

Bank of England

Read analysis

Lombardelli argued that UK labour demand had cooled mainly through lower hiring while dismissals stayed relatively low. Incumbent workers were relatively protected while new entrants faced fewer openings. This cyclical adjustment comes on top of a longer decline in job turnover. Chart 10 shows the quarterly job-to-job switching rate running just over 2% in the preceding year, compared with more than 3% three decades earlier. The age breakdown also shows a disproportionately large contribution from young people to the rise in unemployment since mid-2022.

The policy question is whether job seekers can fill the roles employers have available. If matching has weakened, unemployment can increase without producing the usual restraint on wages. Lombardelli did not infer a material change in equilibrium unemployment from the moderate increases seen so far. Lower mobility could weigh on productivity and slow the reallocation needed to capture AI gains, but the size of those effects remains uncertain.

Questions for further research

  1. How much of the rise in unemployment reflects weaker matching? Decompose job-finding and separation rates by age and sector, and measure vacancy duration and skill mismatch.
  2. Have softer hiring conditions moderated pay in occupations that are still recruiting? Compare pay settlements and vacancy wages for switchers and stayers by sector rather than relying on aggregate earnings.
  3. Where could mobility constraints delay AI-related productivity gains? Compare firm adoption and productivity data with occupations’ hiring, retraining and reassignment patterns.

Monetary Council decision, 17 November 2026

Read analysis

The Council kept the base rate at 5.50% and the overnight corridor at 4.50–6.50%. It reported that headline inflation rose to 2.0% in October, mainly due to fuel, with core at 2.1% and services inflation broadly stable since August. Q3 GDP increased 1.5% from a year earlier, led by industry with a positive contribution from services and a drag from agriculture. The decision leaves the settings unchanged. Its closing paragraph identifies conditions for greater room to act: a favourable domestic risk assessment and inflation outlook that persist, and a less uncertain global environment. The December Inflation Report was identified as the next fuller assessment of those conditions. That is conditional room for policy, with a stable currency still treated as helpful to anchoring expectations.

Bank lending survey – fourth quarter of 2026

Read analysis

The NBP’s October survey of 23 banks found a split between corporate and household credit in the third quarter. Responding banks reported easing business lending standards, mainly because of competition, and reducing margins, non-interest charges and some collateral requirements. They saw stronger demand for financing inventories, working capital and investment. At the same time, household lending standards tightened, particularly for consumer loans. Mortgage demand fell while demand for consumer loans rose by less than business lending demand.

Banks expected corporate and consumer loan demand to increase in Q4 while mortgage demand would remain weak, with limited changes in overall lending policy. The respondents represent about 90% of the sector’s exposures to businesses and households. Responses are weighted by segment market share and describe survey balances and expectations. The reported direction of easing in business credit is evidence about the lending channel rather than a change in the policy rate.

Questions for further research

  1. Did easier corporate credit conditions result in more new lending? Compare new loan volumes and weighted pricing, distinguishing large firms from SMEs and working capital from investment.

2026-11-13ResearchAnalysis available

How accurate are AI models at nowcasting GDP?

Czech National Bank

Read analysis

The CNB authors evaluate short-horizon GDP estimates made at the data cutoff, when some monthly activity indicators are still missing. Since early 2023, the staff forecast combining models and human judgement narrowly outperformed Random Forest against the first GDP release, with a weighted combination of models close behind. They compare predictions across different outcome vintages, reflecting the importance of revisions. They also compare errors against a simple autoregression to help account for changes in overall predictability. In their account, the CNB forecast was around 15% more accurate than that baseline before the pandemic, and almost 35% more accurate in the more recent period.

The authors credit several methods with gains in different regimes and plan to update the weights based on recent accuracy. The comparison reflects their Czech GDP sample. It does not establish that one model will dominate a future cycle, particularly where shocks enter the data with a lag.

Questions for further research

  1. Does the ranking hold when scored against revised GDP? Replicate the study’s vintage-specific RMSE comparison for the same release cutoffs.
  2. Can dynamically fitted weights improve genuinely out-of-sample results? Use rolling estimation with frozen vintages and a held-out period, comparing forecast errors with static weights.
  3. When does judgment add the most value? Compare recorded overrides with mechanical predictions and classify cases by missing data and shock type.

Source sections: CNB blog, sections on evaluation and results, RMSE footnote and forecast-vintage comparison.

Takata sees 2026 as a new stage of normalisation because Japan has again become more exposed to the global cycle and domestic underlying inflation has reached the objective in his assessment. He therefore gives weight to the inflation channel from exchange rates and to the risk of continuing to encourage inflation when the problem is increasingly to anchor it.

His proposed response is a nimble path toward a level sufficiently near neutral to allow moves in either direction. He emphasises structural and external uncertainty about neutral, and rejects binding policy either to fixed increments or to the rate path anticipated by markets. This is the speaker’s view. The edited summary shows different assessments of the costs of waiting. Some views support the hold while the Board assesses earlier tightening, soft spots in activity and weaker consumption momentum. One argument stresses being able to act promptly by bringing the policy rate toward neutral; another stresses several months of observation after each move. 2026-11-07SpeechAnalysis available

Kazuo Ueda: Japan’s Current Account Surplus and Corporate Adjustment

Bank of Japan

Read analysis

Ueda’s central argument is that corporate balance-sheet repair, weak expected domestic returns and outward investment explain Japan’s sustained external surplus better than a simple story about labour scarcity. Firms cut domestic investment after the bubble and prioritised debt reduction, then accumulated buffers or invested overseas. As the stock of foreign assets grew, overseas investment income became more important to the current account than the earlier merchandise-surplus story. Some overseas profits remain abroad despite being counted in Japan’s income and savings statistics.

Demographics matter in this explanation through expectations of a smaller market, even before workers became scarce. For the earlier decades, Ueda points to unused domestic capacity and elevated unemployment as evidence against a simple binding labour-supply explanation. More recently, actual labour shortages are encouraging automation and investment at home. This could narrow excess saving, although large foreign-asset stocks and the return differential could sustain primary income. These are structural channels; the lecture does not announce an imminent rate or exchange-rate decision.

Questions for further research

  1. Will higher domestic investment persist enough to reduce net corporate saving? Compare sector funding balances, firms’ expected domestic returns and realised capital outlays across vintages.
  2. How much does primary income translate into FX demand? Compare reinvested and repatriated earnings against outward investments and FX hedging activity.
  3. Could labour shortages change both the expected return on capital and scale of investment abroad? Distinguish domestic labour-saving capex from cross-border acquisitions by firm size and industry.

Source sections: Official posting dated 7 November; lecture delivered 6 November. §§II–VI and charts 6, 9 and 12–13.

The PBOC retained a moderately loose stance and described a recovery with first-three-quarter growth of 4.6% year on year, but with supply still stronger than demand and uneven sector performance. It set out three channels: ample system liquidity, lower all-in financing costs and targeted support to selected activities. Among targeted changes were a 25 basis point reduction in the pledged supplementary lending rate and additional lending capacity for technology and small businesses. An authorised programme ceiling is a facility parameter rather than evidence that funds were drawn.

The operating chapter explains why the switch to a daily fixed-rate overnight reverse repo matters. It narrows the distance between the policy instrument’s maturity and overnight traded funding. The report describes a 1.25% overnight operation rate from the new daily framework and a separate seven-day tender principally around liquidity pressure points. It reports earlier injections through several longer tools to offset drains including tax and bond issuance. The policy outlook emphasises stronger countercyclical adjustment, flexible timing and a managed RMB float with protection against overshooting. These are the bank’s outlook and reported operations as of publication.

Questions for further research

  1. Does the overnight framework reduce liquidity dislocations? Compare DR001, DR007 and their dispersion during matched tax dates and month-ends, adjusting for government cash flows.
  2. Does cheaper or targeted funding reach businesses facing weak demand? Check tool drawdowns, effective rates and fee disclosures for borrowers rather than programme limits alone.
  3. Is credit formation broadening beyond policy-supported sectors? Review the composition of aggregate financing and private loan demand alongside quarterly data on private investment and household spending.

Source sections: PBOC original report on Shanghai government host. See executive summary, Part II §1 and the policy outlook. The original report was disseminated 11 November, before Shanghai’s republication.

Coverage: Analysis covers the executive summary, main operations and policy outlook. Detailed tables and appendices were not independently checked.

Earlier spring holds had allowed the Board to assess how the Middle East and commodity-price developments would affect Korea. Its discussion of corporate bonds refers separately to spreads and their investor-demand drivers. Questions for further research

2026-11-11ResearchAnalysis available

AI and Regional Labor Markets

Bank of Korea

Read analysis

The staff study estimates occupational and regional exposure separately for generative, agentic and physical AI. It finds more concentration of generative and agentic exposure in metropolitan Seoul and other centres for knowledge services, while several manufacturing and agricultural regions have relatively higher exposure to physical AI. In early observations, employment grew faster in occupations with higher generative or agentic exposure, driven by the metropolitan area. Occupational composition both determines measured exposure and can explain different regional employment outcomes. The authors explicitly caution that early regional associations do not establish that AI caused changes in employment.

The distinction is useful when assessing whether a technology-led upswing in output is broadly shared. Regional purchasing power, migration and occupations can respond differently even if nationwide productivity improves. The November posting is the English-language edition and should not be dated or treated as newly released Korean evidence without checking the original publication.

Questions for further research

  1. Does exposure translate to realised adoption and productivity? Track uptake and measured output by occupation and region, allowing for task and firm composition.
  2. Are regions following different pre-existing growth paths? Test pre-trends in regional hiring before AI adoption and compare the same occupations across regions.
  3. How do gains in knowledge occupations compare with pressures in production jobs? Compare vacancies, worker flows and wage growth by AI category exposure rather than using employment stocks alone.

Source sections: Official English research summary and linked BOK Issue Note 2026-25; Korean edition appeared in September.

Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas

Read analysis

The authors find that tighter global financial conditions are associated with Philippine firms shifting their funding mix towards domestic currency. Their indicators capture different forces: the US federal funds rate measures a funding-cost channel, dollar movements and volatility capture exchange-rate risks, and the VIX measures market volatility. The analysis combines an aggregate lag model for external debt with firm-level panel estimates of debt composition and local projections for firm performance. External debt is an imperfect proxy for foreign-currency debt. The paper’s footnote describes the prevalence of foreign currency within measured external debt.

The estimated funding shift varies across firms. For example, the paper reports a greater propensity to shift towards domestic currency among several globally oriented and manufacturing firms, with globally oriented firms starting from greater foreign-currency exposure. The authors treat firm size and access to local funding as possible explanations for uneven adjustment. Those patterns matter because the ability to refinance in pesos may vary substantially across borrowers.

Higher US policy rates are associated with larger interest expenses and weaker net income. Dollar volatility is associated with lower interest expense and stronger net income for some firms. The authors view those results as consistent with firms adapting their financing, while recognising uncertainty and limited firm coverage. Figure 5.1 presents estimated responses with confidence intervals for separate income measures and levels of FX debt. The panels use different vertical scales. The estimates do not establish that realised funding changes caused later performance outcomes. These are research findings attributed to the authors rather than a BSP policy decision.

Questions for further research

  1. How much of the funding adjustment depends on debt maturities and bank access? Use currency-by-maturity loan and bond data and compare firms with similar initial FX exposure.
  2. Would exchange-rate hedges change which firms are vulnerable? Combine currency-matched revenues and derivative positions with debt schedules and financing terms.
  3. Can a domestic funding buffer help smaller or unlisted firms? Seek broader administrative loan data to test whether the sample’s adjustment is representative.
  4. Can the Fed funding-cost channel be separated from other global shocks? Compare higher-frequency identified surprises with the authors’ proxy specifications and test lag and sample sensitivity.

Source sections: BSP Discussion Paper 2026-08, manuscript dated October and featured online on 3 November. Selected read of §§ IV–VI, Tables 5.1 and 5.3, Figure 5.1 and the external-debt proxy footnote.

Edited Minutes of the Monetary Policy Committee Meeting No. 5/2026

Bank of Thailand

Read analysis

The minutes released 11 November cover the October meeting and explain why the MPC retained accommodation amid stronger activity in some sectors. The committee attributed much of the stronger outlook to technology-linked manufacturing exports and investment and judged the distribution of gains narrow. The minutes note that revised manufacturing coverage affects estimates of recent momentum and that historical GDP revisions could affect year-on-year comparisons.

For inflation, energy subsidies reduced the forecast compared with the previous projection despite higher global oil prices. The committee identified the Oil Fuel Fund’s financial capacity as a risk to future cushioning and watched for higher input costs passing through to core prices. External reserves were cited as a buffer against funding volatility. Domestic credit remained uneven: rising loans to larger borrowers coexisted with weak SME credit. Members discussed targeted interventions because an aggregate policy rate cannot directly resolve structural barriers to credit.

Questions for further research

  1. How sensitive is the inflation forecast to the Oil Fuel Fund’s ability to cushion energy costs? Compare the minutes’ assumptions with the fund’s financial statements and retail fuel price schedules.
  2. How much of the growth revision survives methodological changes? Reconcile old and revised output and manufacturing vintages, keeping growth rates and levels distinct.
  3. Which targeted measures can reach borrowers facing credit rationing? Track eligible SME borrowing, risk grades and arrears before and after changes in guarantee or lending programmes.

Source sections: Edited minutes pp. 1–4, especially the inflation outlook, financial conditions and monetary policy considerations.

Minutes of the November 2026 Monetary Policy Board meeting

Reserve Bank of Australia

Read analysis

The minutes explain the six-to-three vote to raise the cash rate to 4.85%. The majority saw more persistent inflation, greater risk to expectations and tentative resilience in employment and household balance sheets. It put more weight on the risk that an insufficiently restrictive rate would let inflation expectations rise. Staff had revised their view of supply capacity, while stable wage growth and the slowdown in wages on individual arrangements were counterpoints to the assessment of a still-tight labour market.

The three members who preferred to hold wanted to assess the effect of the 100 basis points of tightening already delivered. They saw greater risk of a sharper downturn and rising unemployment. The split identifies which evidence could change votes, while the Board as a whole retained a data-dependent approach. The minutes report the 3 November decision, so measure any price response to these details separately from the original announcement.

Questions for further research

  1. What does the November split imply about sensitivity to jobs data? Compare the published arguments with wages, vacancies and employment indicators and observe subsequent changes in short-rate pricing.
  2. Do the measures of expectations tell a common story? Compare business surveys with household surveys and market compensation at several maturities, allowing for each measure’s limits.
  3. Did anyone learn something tradeable on 17 November? Compare before and after OIS quotes at the minutes release, with simultaneous announcements flagged.

Source sections: Meeting held 3 November, minutes released 17 November. Considerations for monetary policy and The decision

Read analysis

Bullock emphasises upside inflation risks after five rate increases totalling 125 basis points in 2026. She says higher oil prices add to inflation that was already above target before the Middle East shock. The forecast uses an oil futures curve that implies easing, while she notes that previous expectations of falling oil prices had not materialised. She also cites tentative business liaison evidence that longer exposure to high inflation may be changing firms’ beliefs about its normal level.

She describes productivity changes as a potential help to the economy alongside operational challenges, and notes uneven household exposure to the cost of living. The monetary signal is a continued focus on inflation persistence, with attention to the limitations of the oil assumption and early signs in expectations. The panel contains other speakers, whose comments are outside this Governor-focused readout. The November minutes were released later that morning, a separate event on any same-day chart.

Questions for further research

  1. Is the oil forecast vulnerable to refined-product bottlenecks? Compare dated crude and refined-product curves and track freight and refining constraints.
  2. Is the change in business beliefs broad or concentrated? Compare survey distributions and reported pricing plans across sectors rather than extrapolating from isolated liaison comments.
  3. What information came from the panel versus the minutes? Compare intraday price changes around the separately scheduled events and flag other releases.

2026-11-09SpeechAnalysis available

Sarah Hunter: What Happens to the Economy as ‘Intelligence’ Gets Cheaper?

Reserve Bank of Australia

Read analysis

Hunter examines the timing mismatch between AI investment, which raises demand immediately, and broader productive gains, which take time and vary widely across studies. Near-term investment runs into limited capacity in data centres, technology goods and complementary inputs. The speech’s cross-country price charts show stronger increases in several exposed goods, especially in the United States, while the theoretical framework allows rising supply to relieve those bottlenecks over time.

The speech also distinguishes the effects of AI on the level of real activity, inflation and the neutral rate. Stronger investment demand could raise the neutral rate, but the range is wide and depends on diffusion, the labour market and households’ response. Stronger demand can eventually accompany stronger productive capacity, so favourable productivity is compatible with a broadly neutral longer-run effect on inflation. Hunter presents channels and uncertainties rather than a short-term rate call.

Questions for further research

  1. Which bottlenecks are visible in Australia’s prices today? Compare affected CPI components with import unit values, domestic construction costs and investment plans.
  2. What would demonstrate a persistent productive-capacity gain? Look for output per hour and adoption changes outside technology producers and early adopters.
  3. Would a higher neutral rate alter interpretation of long yields? Compare model estimates and investment scenarios against the neutral-rate range in the speech.

Source sections: Diagram of economic channels, Inflation section, neutral rate estimates and Conclusion

Andrew Hauser: Trust, Expectations and Monetary Policy

Reserve Bank of Australia

Read analysis

Hauser argues that trust changes how strongly and quickly monetary policy affects expected future conditions and spending today. In Graph 1, the model holds the realised cash-rate path fixed. Output and inflation fall sooner and further when the tightening is anticipated. Graph 2 turns the question around: after a temporary foreign cost shock, achieving the same inflation path can require less tightening and a smaller GDP loss if people expect the central bank to return inflation to target promptly.

He cites firm survey responses linking expectations of timely disinflation to intended restraint in cost pass-through. Graph 3 presents an association between household trust in the RBA and lower near-term inflation expectations. The surveys and simulations show different kinds of evidence and do not establish a realised causal effect for a particular speech. His conclusion is that clarity, accountability and demonstrated delivery matter for credibility, especially after a prolonged period of elevated inflation.

Questions for further research

  1. Which expectations measure best tracks the pass-through mechanism? Match firm-level planned price increases to their inflation and trust answers and check for composition effects.
  2. Can communication alter expectations without a rate move? Compare changes around communication events across market pricing and survey waves, accounting for simultaneous news.
  3. Is the trust relationship stable in large cost shocks? Test the survey relationships across industries with different exposure to input costs and demand.

Source sections: Graphs 1–3, evidence on trust and concluding discussion

2026-11-03ForecastAnalysis available

Statement on Monetary Policy, November 2026

Reserve Bank of Australia

Read analysis

The November Statement revises the inflation outlook upwards and delays the forecast return to the target band. Its outlook combines persistent domestic capacity pressure with higher oil and refined-product prices and resilient global demand connected to AI investment. Restrictive financial conditions are expected to keep growth below potential for a period, creating spare capacity and allowing inflation to fall. The forecast uses data through 28 October.

The staff’s oil assumptions illustrate the extent of the shock: the December-quarter level is 35% higher than in the August forecast, and by end-2028 it is 11% higher. Graph 3.1 compares the paths as assumptions. The cash-rate assumption is a market path, which rises by 35 basis points by mid-2027 and then eases a little before levelling near 4.8% in 2028. Its higher level than in August is part of the forecast conditioning, rather than a Board pledge. Staff also note that higher long real yields could mean less policy restraint if they signal higher neutral rates, or tighter conditions if they mainly reflect higher term premia. This entry focuses on the forecast and its assumptions.

Questions for further research

  1. How far would a persistent fuel-cost shock delay disinflation? Use the RBA’s risk scenarios and compare dated crude and refined-fuel curves with its conditioning assumptions.
  2. Can we disentangle neutral-rate repricing from term premia? Compare short-rate expectations, longer real yields and term-premium estimates, acknowledging model uncertainty.
  3. Does restrictive policy transmit as forecast? Track mortgage resets, credit growth and business investment with an August-to-November forecast comparison.

Source sections: Overview and Outlook, especially Graph 3.1, the conditioning assumptions and forecast tables

2026-11-03DecisionAnalysis available

Monetary Policy Board decision: cash rate raised to 4.85%

Reserve Bank of Australia

Read analysis

The Board raised the cash rate target by 25 basis points to 4.85%, by six votes to three. The three preferred 4.60%. The statement judged inflation broad-based and the forecast materially worse than before. Higher fuel and commodity prices mattered, alongside tighter-than-estimated domestic capacity, higher AI-related technology goods prices and business reports of continuing cost pass-through. The Board said inflation was now expected to reach the top of the 2–3% target band in late 2027, roughly three quarters later than previously forecast.

The decision tightens the current setting, while the split shows the Board did not agree on the need for another move at this meeting. The statement makes further decisions conditional on incoming data, the outlook and risks. The investment question is whether incoming evidence will require more restraint than the future path markets already price. The release provides the policy decision and forecast revision, while price observations around publication are needed to assess the surprise.

Questions for further research

  1. What drove the first change in short-rate pricing? Compare AUD overnight-indexed swaps and bills immediately around publication. The November forecast was released at the same time.
  2. Are weak labour conditions beginning to limit pass-through? Compare local services inflation, vacancies, unemployment and liaison evidence on selling-price plans.
  3. Which oil assumptions are most important for the forecast timing? Compare the Statement on Monetary Policy’s conditioning assumptions with Brent and refined-product futures on 3 November.

Source sections: Media release, opening paragraphs and Decision

Michele Bullock: November monetary policy media conference

Reserve Bank of Australia

Read analysis

Bullock said the Board raised the cash rate to 4.85% because domestic capacity pressures and inflation persistence required more restraint. She distinguishes the direct rise in global oil prices from domestic demand and the effect higher costs could have on expectations and firms’ selling prices. She points to weak productivity and unexpectedly strong data-centre-related investment. Earlier tightening had already slowed spending, reduced housing prices and eased the labour market, but she expected further moderation to be needed.

In the Q&A, Bullock discusses a policy transmission lag of around a year or potentially more and describes housing as one channel whose interpretation is complicated by other policy changes. She said the RBA takes public demand as given in assessing aggregate demand. The press conference starts after the concurrent decision and projections, giving a distinct period in which to look for incremental information in her explanation.

Questions for further research

  1. Did the Q&A move pricing after the initial decision? Align market data with the decision at 2.30 pm AEDT and press conference at 3.30 pm AEDT, then isolate material remarks.
  2. How much do revisions to domestic capacity matter relative to fuel? Compare the forecast changes, trimmed-mean inflation and activity indicators with earlier releases.
  3. Is the latest tightening already affecting housing beyond other policy changes? Compare credit, prices and household cash flows across regions and cohorts with different rate sensitivity.

Financial Stability Report, November 2026

Reserve Bank of New Zealand

Read analysis

The Reserve Bank assesses the domestic system as resilient, backed by capital and liquidity buffers, while judging global risks to have risen. Export income and easing mortgage pressure had reduced financial stress overall, but weakness in some businesses and higher import and funding costs could reverse the improvement. The report highlights a route from geopolitical or AI valuation shocks into New Zealand through trading-partner demand, business confidence and banks’ offshore funding. Its discussion of AI points to concentration, interconnected financing and debt as possible amplifiers if expected returns disappoint.

Deposits remain an important and typically stable funding source, but faster switching between institutions could make funding more rate-sensitive, with different implications in normal conditions and stress. The report also considers operational resilience and stress-test results. Investment implications are conditional: an international market repricing could affect NZ bank funding and domestic credit even if local household exposure to overseas equities were relatively small. No policy rate decision is contained in this report.

Questions for further research

  1. How vulnerable is bank funding to an offshore spread shock? Compare wholesale maturity profiles, cross-currency funding costs and domestic deposit competition.
  2. Which local borrowers are most exposed to reversal of the recent improvement? Track stress and refinancing separately for households, exporters and firms facing imported input costs.
  3. Does easier digital deposit switching raise realised outflow risk? Compare the distribution of deposit tenure and repricing behaviour with the report’s stress assumptions.

Source sections: Financial stability at a glance, chapter 1, and deposit behaviour discussion

Paul Conway: How is the New Zealand economy tracking?

Reserve Bank of New Zealand

Read analysis

Conway explained his own October vote for a 25 basis point hike while the committee held the OCR at 2.75%. He and the other dissenters put more weight on high core inflation and rising breadth than the hold voters, who wanted time to see the effect of previous increases on an uneven domestic recovery. He characterised the vote as a difference about the timing and risk management of a shared, conditional tightening direction.

He noted that subsequently released labour data were relatively weak and that oil prices and regional AI-related equity valuations had fallen. This matters for interpreting an earlier affirmative hike vote: the new evidence could change the balance between persistence and weaker demand, and the speech does not promise the next vote. Conway’s presentation also makes clear what is extrapolation: the previous 4.4% fourth-quarter inflation projection used oil futures at the time of the October review.

Questions for further research

  1. How much did lower oil prices change the path implicit in the October projection? Compare the futures curve on the review date with the curve at the time of Conway’s remarks and track the exchange rate.
  2. Could weak hiring alter the timing of the next move? Check labour market quantities, wages and investment intentions for sustained weakening beyond one release.
  3. Was Conway’s personal willingness to tighten new information? Compare the speech to the named October vote and examine instrument-specific pricing shortly before and after the remarks.

Source sections: Speaking notes, slides 2–5 and discussion of the outlook
